Monday, 8 March. Town hall of the 4th arrondissement. Julien has come to register Rose-Hélène’s birth. At the counter is the very clerk who prepared their wedding, Théo’s mother.
Mr Moreau! What a surprise! Théo told me the baby was born during his concert. That’s the reason he’s talked about nothing else since Thursday.
(laughs) It’s true. He played the waltz to the end, and my wife waited for the last note. I’ve come to register the birth.
Very good. Do you have the maternity certificate and the family booklet, the one I wrote your marriage in?
Yes, here they are. And my wife’s ID, without which, she told me, I wasn’t allowed to leave the house.
She’s right. Right, the first name? Is the one you thought of still Rose-Hélène?
Yes, with a hyphen. Rose, like my grandmother, and Hélène, like a very dear friend to whom we owe a lot.
Madame Morel? The lady for whom 3 May was chosen? I remember very well. She had a superb hat.
That’s her. She cried when we told her the name.
(types on the computer) Done. Rose-Hélène Moreau, born on 4 March at 3:12. I’m adding her to the page of the booklet where your marriage already is. Any other questions?
Yes, one. We’d like to hold an Orthodox baptism in Romania this summer. Are there French documents we’ll need?
Just an extract of the birth certificate, which I’ll give you right away. And the godfather and godmother, have you chosen them?
In Romanian tradition they’re the wedding godparents, the ones with whom you walked around the altar. So our friends Karim and Leïla.
It’s a lovely tradition. In France people often choose a brother or a sister.
Exactly, that’s the problem I hadn’t thought of. My brother-in-law Radu absolutely wants to be godfather. And my sister Manon wants to be godmother.
(laughs) Then you’ll have four godparents. Your daughter will be the best-protected little girl in Lyon!

"Luh-kel" / "la-kel". The plural "lesquels" = "lay-kel", the s is silent.
"Ba-tem": the P is NOT pronounced! Likewise "baptiser" = "ba-tee-zay".
"Fee-yuhl": godson. The feminine "filleule" sounds the same.
"Tray-dew-nyon": the hyphen. "Rose-Hélène" is written with a trait d’union.
After a preposition (avec, dans, pour, sur, sans, sous, par, entre…) you can’t use "que". You use LEQUEL, which agrees with the noun, like English "which / in which / with which":
The booklet in which I wrote your marriage.
The document without which I wasn’t allowed to leave.
The reason why he talks about nothing else.
The friends with whom we walked around the altar.
For people, "qui" can also be used after a preposition: "les amis avec qui on a…", "la dame pour qui…". It’s even more common in speech.
With the preposition "à", lequel contracts, like the article (à + le = au):
The first name you thought of.
The problem I hadn’t thought of.
The meeting I took part in.
For PEOPLE, with "à" you use "à qui": "une amie à qui nous devons beaucoup" (not "à laquelle", though it’s possible). For THINGS: "auquel / à laquelle".
With verbs taking "de" (parler de, avoir besoin de), you use "dont" (ch. 21). But with PHRASES ending in "de" (près de, à côté de, au milieu de, en face de, au bout de) you use DUQUEL / DE LAQUELLE:
les papiers dont nous aurons besoin
la maison près de laquelle j’habite
le parc au milieu duquel il y a un lac
the park in the middle of which there’s a lake
Contractions: de + lequel = duquel, de + lesquels = desquels, de + lesquelles = desquelles. But: de laquelle (no contraction).
l’employée qui a préparé le mariage
la mairie où nous nous sommes mariés

On the first truly warm day of spring, at the end of March, Ioana decided that Rose-Hélène was ready for her first big outing. The destination she had been thinking of for weeks was obvious: the care home at Fourvière, where everyone was waiting impatiently for the baby.

All four of them set off: Ioana, Julien, the grandmother and the pram in which Rose-Hélène slept, bundled up in the pink bonnet Brigitte had knitted. The funicular, which they boarded at the Saint-Jean station, was full of tourists smiling at the baby.

Hélène was waiting for them at the entrance, by the railing behind which the building site could be seen. She had put on her most beautiful dress, the one she had worn to the wedding, and the mărțișor the grandmother had given her. The two old ladies hugged like two sisters who hadn’t seen each other in years.

In the common room a surprise awaited them. The residents had decorated the room with paper garlands and a big sign on which they had written, in clumsy letters: "Welcome, Rose-Hélène!" Madame Lambert, the former schoolteacher, had led the work. She had corrected the spelling of the name three times.

Monsieur Petit, the former postman, came over with his walking frame. In his hand he held a small cardboard box, inside which was a collection of old postcards of Lyon. "I delivered them for forty years," he explained. "These are the most beautiful ones. They’re for the little one, when she can read."

The lady from Valencia, the one to whom Lucia had sung the Spanish song, had embroidered a small handkerchief with the initials R. H. A gentleman who never spoke and whose story nobody really knew put on the table a tiny blue jumper, which he had knitted himself, in secret, all winter.

Ioana was so moved that she didn’t know what to say. She took Rose-Hélène out of the pram and introduced her to each resident, one by one. Some held her in their arms. Others just looked at her, with shining eyes. Rose-Hélène slept through almost the whole visit, which greatly impressed Madame Lambert.

Then Ioana showed the whole family the building site. It was the first time the grandmother had seen the project her granddaughter had been working on for a year. The walls of the Salle Henri Bernard were up, and the large windows, through which the garden could already be seen, had just been fitted.

Ioana pointed out the exact spot where the small stage, Lucia’s idea, would be installed. Then the corner near which the piano would go. "The inauguration will take place in September," she explained. "The work is a little behind, but we’ll make it."

The grandmother slowly walked around the room, touching the walls, as if she wanted to check they were solid. Then she said something in Romanian, and Ioana translated for Hélène: "She says she’s proud of me. And that she doesn’t understand how a little girl who was afraid of the dark can build such big things."

Hélène smiled. She took the grandmother’s hand. They stood for a moment in the middle of the empty room, the two of them, the Frenchwoman and the Romanian, the one who had waited sixty years for a pianist and the one who had danced for fifty years with the best dancer in her village.

The following week, the grandmother took the coach back to Iași. She had stayed a month, exactly as she had announced. In that month she had cooked every day, rocked Rose-Hélène every night and taught Lucia three recipes without which, according to her, no Romanian family can survive.

Everyone was at the coach station: Ioana with the baby, Julien, Radu, Lucia, Madame Bernard and even Hélène, who had insisted on coming. The driver was the same as on the way there: Costel, the one with whom the grandmother had talked for thirty hours. He greeted her like an old friend.

Before getting on the coach, the grandmother hugged everyone, for a long time. She kissed Rose-Hélène last, on the forehead, and whispered something in her ear. Ioana didn’t hear the words. She never asked. There are sentences for which a translation would be too much.

When the coach left, Radu took Lucia’s hand, and Julien took Ioana’s. Hélène waved her handkerchief until the coach disappeared round the corner of the street. Then she turned to Madame Bernard. "You know, Odile, I think I’ve just lost a friend with whom I could never exchange a single sentence. And yet she’s one of the best I’ve ever had."

That evening, the flat seemed too big and too quiet. There was no longer the smell of soup simmering since morning, nor the Romanian songs with which the grandmother put the baby to sleep. Victor wandered around the kitchen, looking for the person he had been begging for scraps of meat for a month.

When Ioana opened the fridge, she let out a little cry. It was full. Boxes everywhere, on which the grandmother had stuck labels in Romanian: "sarmale – Monday", "ciorbă – Tuesday", "plăcinte – for Radu, if he’s good". There was enough food for two weeks.

At the back of the fridge, behind the boxes, there was an envelope. Inside, a little letter written with great care, in which the grandmother had tried to write in French, with the help of a dictionary: "My Ioana. You are a good mum. Sleep a little. Eat. I’m coming back in August for the baptism. Granny."

Ioana read the letter three times. Then she showed it to Julien, who smiled. "Six words of French in a week," he said. "She’s learning faster than I’m learning Romanian." Ioana put the letter in the baby’s diary, on the page where she had written, two weeks earlier, on the day the grandmother arrived. She knew it was a letter she would reread all her life.

That night, for the first time, Rose-Hélène slept through the night. Ioana woke at seven, frightened, and ran to the cot. The baby was sleeping peacefully, fists clenched. Julien said it was surely the grandmother’s last gift.
